data.title: Hronský Beňadik – a Slavic hillfort on Beňadická skala
data.excerpt: Between 1972 and 1977, rampart features unrecorded in the archaeological literature – and missed even by Janšák’s inventory of the Hron region – were noticed on a prominent rise some 700 m south of the former monastery at Hronský Beňadik. Excavation identified a 10th-century Slavic hillfort of about 2.28 ha that guarded the road along the Hron, one of four to five fortified points controlling a stretch just under 7 km long.

children.text: The site

Between 1972 and 1977, rampart features that had not until then been recorded in the archaeological literature could be observed in the terrain on a prominent rise at Hronský Beňadik, at a distance of about 700 m south of the precinct of the former monastery. Nor had Janšák recorded this place in his inventory of sites in the Hron region. An archaeological excavation was therefore carried out, which made it possible to date the site and to identify it as a Slavic hillfort.

The fortified area of the hillfort lies on the right bank of the Hron between the villages of Hronský Beňadik and Psiare. It extends over an elongated tongue-shaped spur with an area of approximately 2.28 ha. The maximum length of the fortified area is 360 m, the maximum width about 80–90 m. This area slopes down to the south towards the village of Psiare, the slope dropping 25 m over a length of 350 m. The elevation is 200–228 m above sea level.

children.text: The area is artificially enclosed only on the northern side and at the north-western corner. The entire eastern perimeter is protected by a steep drop, which once fell away into the bed of the Hron; today the main course of the river has shifted further to the east, and the Zvolen–Levice road and the railway line run below the hillfort. On the western side the hillfort is protected in its northern part by a rampart construction and in the southern part by a deep gully, which joins the valley of the Hron below the southern spur of the hillfort.
The fortification

At the highest point of the hillfort, in the immediate vicinity of the rampart fortification, stands a Baroque sacral building of 1713. According to written sources, the chapel stands on the site of an earlier building, probably of timber, which was dedicated to St Helena. The present building has the patrocinium of the Holy Cross (the Finding of the Holy Cross). The rampart fortification begins to the north of the present chapel and runs in a ground plan of approximately a quarter-circle to the west and then to the south. 85 running metres of the fortification have survived (measured along the crown of the rampart). The continuation of the rampart to the south and its junction with the natural fall of the gully is interrupted by a field track; the continuation of the rampart on the other side towards the east was destroyed by a path and by landscaping around the chapel, which serves as a place of pilgrimage. On the inner side the rampart reaches a height of about 1.5 m from the foot of the rampart, on the outside in places as much as 6 m from the present bottom of the ditch. In the middle of the western perimeter of the hillfort, part of the rampart fortification was destroyed after the Second World War and its mass pushed into the gully. Today the rampart is spread out to a width of 14 m; originally its width from the foot to the outer face of the stone wall was about 6 m.

The fortification consisted of an outer drystone wall 60–80 cm thick, behind which, towards the interior of the hillfort, there was an earthen fortification reinforced at least in places by a timber (beam?) construction. Of the timber parts of the construction only traces of horizontal rotted beams have survived, which were covered by many layers of soil in various shades of colour, from brownish-yellow through brownish-orange and grey to dark brown and black. The uppermost layer also contained quarried stones, probably from the upper part of the stone wall. It was not possible to establish in these places how the upper part of the rampart was originally finished.
The finds

Within the area of the hillfort, the remains of dwellings with a heating installation were found, some of which probably had a log construction. From the material culture, a large number of pottery sherds from the period shortly after the demise of Great Moravia were found. The decorative elements consist exclusively of simple wavy lines, oblique fingernail incisions below the neck of the vessels and horizontal grooving on the lower parts. From the larger quantity of pottery fragments it proved possible to reconstruct five complete vessels and one partially, while of a rare flask-shaped vessel only the rim with the neck has survived. The reconstructed vessels belong to the same type: all are pot-shaped with a slightly ovoid body and a funnel-shaped flaring mouth. The marks on the bases consist exclusively of circles and crosses. Evidence of craft production was also provided by an undamaged quern runner stone with a diameter of 43 cm. An unfinished runner stone was also found, as well as a larger quantity of stone fragments, which testifies to the production of querns on the site. The material was probably brought in from nearby Žarnovica or its immediate surroundings. Several fragments of iron objects (a sickle, a knife, an arrowhead) were also found here. The occupation was concentrated within the hillfort at the foot of the rampart along its perimeter, while the interior spaces of the hillfort were left free – evidently in order to secure an emergency refuge for a larger number of inhabitants in times of threat.

An important question is the location of the original entrance into the hillfort. Despite test trenching at several places where an entrance could be expected, it was not possible to locate the site of the gateway. The present entrances are probably adaptations of later centuries. The path from the north evidently came into being through centuries of pilgrimage to the chapel, while the track from the west was intended for agricultural machinery and carts. In the southern part of the western perimeter, a broad area resembling a deserted medieval road from the south, from the village of Psiare, reaches into the area of the hillfort. The road climbed gradually up the gully and then up the line of steepest slope towards the hillfort. The excavation uncovered no traces of a gateway along the course of this presumed road, but none of a destroyed rampart either, and so it is not possible to judge with certainty whether the road was used during the existence of the hillfort or came into being only after its demise.
The dating of the hillfort and its probable function

The hillfort lost its defensive function long ago and its fortification has disintegrated over a thousand years; a tradition has survived, however, in the existence of a sacral building. The present chapel, which was built at the beginning of the 18th century, continued an earlier building. Although the patrocinium of the chapel changed, among the inhabitants of the wider area the custom of going on pilgrimage „k Jelenke“ (to Jelenka) survived until recently. The form of the name Jelena instead of Elena or Helena testifies to a very old tradition. Although it was not possible to establish the remains of an earlier sacral building, one may be assumed here as early as the time of the foundation of the Benedictine monastery at Hronský Beňadik, even though it is not explicitly mentioned in the donation charter of 1075.

On the basis of the finds from the archaeological excavation, the hillfort on Beňadická skala can be dated to the 10th century. As at other hillforts in the area of the middle Hron region, it was confirmed that the areas of post-Great Moravian hillforts were not occupied in their entirety, but that the occupation was concentrated only in the vicinity of the rampart. No evidence could be obtained about the use of the central area of the hillfort. It was probably a reserve, intended to provide a refuge for the population of the surrounding lowlands in case of danger.

Important finds are the objects documenting the occupations of the population at the hillfort. A sickle, a ploughshare and querns testify to agricultural production. The querns were made on the site itself. The pottery was evidently brought in from nearby settlements on the plain in the floodplain of the Hron. Spindle whorls and small iron knives were, until recently, everyday objects in every rural household. The character of the hillfort was, however, primarily military. The spur and the arrowhead certainly did not reach the area of the hillfort by chance. The massive fortification and the advanced position of the hillfort demonstrate its importance as a guardian of the road along the Hron, and possibly also of the ford to the other bank, where the Slavs made use of the extensive prehistoric hillfort on the rock of Krivín. The only shortcoming of the hillfort was the problem of supplying drinking water. Transporting water from the valley of the Hron was probably not very advantageous, especially during a siege. A weak spring does rise from the rock above the Hronský Beňadik–Psiare road (today a statue of St John of Nepomuk stands on that spot), but during the existence of the hillfort access to the spring from the occupied area would have been possible only by rope ladders. Another spring on the slope between the building of the Benedictine monastery and the hillfort could easily have been occupied by an enemy. The hillfort was evidently not occupied for very long. If it came into being at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries, it certainly no longer served its purpose in the 11th century, when a more advantageous place in present-day Hronský Beňadik was settled. On its site, in the second half of the 11th century, the Benedictine monastery arose, with a densely settled surrounding area.
The hillfort on Beňadická skala formed part of a system of hillforts in the Hron region in the area of the Slovenská brána (the Slovak Gate).

The hillforts of Grác on the hill of Pipíška near Malé Kozmálovce, Hrádze (Festunok) near Tlmače, Krivín in the cadastral area of Rybník opposite the village of Psiare (today part of the municipality of Hronský Beňadik), and possibly also a further hillfort above Kozárovce destroyed by a quarry, were contemporary and had the same function: to protect the road along the Hron and the fords in this area. Four to five fortified points controlled a territory just under 7 km long. This fact too demonstrates that the area of central Slovakia to the north of these hillforts was not empty of people before the 11th century, as some Hungarian historians claimed until recently. The surroundings were densely settled, as also follows from the list of estates that Géza I granted to the monastery at Hronský Beňadik in 1075.

The archaeological excavation at the Beňadik hillfort produced results surprisingly consistent with the results of the excavation at the hillfort of Hrádze at Tlmače. In both cases the guard and defensive character of the hillfort is complemented by a large reserve of space in the middle of the fortified area, which served as a refuge for the population of the immediate surroundings. Unlike other contemporary hillforts in the Slovenská brána, however, the hillfort on Beňadická skala came into being on a site not occupied until then, perhaps as a pendant to the much more extensive hillfort on Krivín opposite.

The fortified line on the right bank of the Hron was evidently well known at that time, and awareness of it persisted into the following centuries. Only thus can one explain the words of the Prague canon Cosmas, who as late as the 12th century writes that the Hron was the eastern border of Svatopluk's realm in the 9th century. It is more probable, however, that

the Slavic hillforts in this stretch of the Hron region came into being only in the 10th century and were intended to halt the advance of the Magyars, who were penetrating from the south along the Hron into the mountainous areas of central Slovakia. In the event of raids, the hillforts provided a refuge and were also a place where local warriors gathered.

Such an explanation fully corresponds to the information on Slavic hillforts as given in the 11th century by the Arab writer Gardizi, who worked up older accounts from the 10th century. According to Gardizi, the Slavs used their forts in times of danger; they inhabited them mainly in winter, while in summer they lived outside them.

After the emergence of the Kingdom of Hungary and the incorporation of central Slovakia into its organisation, the Hron region hillforts lost their justification and came to an end. In their place, settlements in the Hron lowland grew. The territory once controlled by the hillforts did not lose its importance, however, and perhaps it was precisely for that reason that this place was chosen for the foundation of the Benedictine monastery in present-day Hronský Beňadik.
The marking and present state of the hillfort

You can reach the hillfort quickly and comfortably along a narrow path that begins by the cross beside the main road between Hronský Beňadik and the village of Psiare. As can be seen in the photographs, the area of the hillfort is a very fine level surface, with an almost vertical face on the western side. The route to the hillfort is not marked in any way, and within the area of the hillfort you will not find a trace of any information panel from which you might learn that you are standing on a Slavic hillfort. On the north-eastern side the rampart is still clearly visible.
